texts.preamble: In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 In The Court Of Sh. Ashu Garg, Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate - Ii (New Delhi), Patiala House Courts, New Delhi Cc No. 46/10 (44390/16) Unique Case Id No. 02403R0064712010 Date of Institution: 25.02.2010 Date of reserving judgement: 19.10.2016 Date of pronouncement: 19.10.2016 In re: Delhi Administration / Food Inspector Department of Pfa, Govt. of Nct of Delhi A-20, Lawrence Road Industrial Area, Delhi-110 035 ... Complainant versus A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja [Since Acquitted] A-2) Amit Kanojia [Since Acquitted] A-3) M/s. Fun Food Pvt. Ltd. [Since Acquitted] A-4) Mukul Parakh S/o. Sh. K. C. Parakh R/o. 5-C, Duplex Colony, Near Medical College, Bikaner, Rajasthan. A-5) M/s. Three Vees Village Pratap Pur, Tehsil Kashi Pur, Distt. Udham Singh Nagar, Uttarakhand ... Accused Persons Cc No. 46/10 Page 1 of 13 Judgment:
texts.facts: Fun Food Pvt. Ltd. 1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (PFA Act), alleging that the accused persons have violated the provisions of the PFA Act and Rules. The accused no.1 is stated to be the vendor-cum-proprietor of M/s. National General Store from where the food article, that is, 'Culinary Sauce' was lifted for sampling. Accused no.3 is stated to be In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/ 1 the Company, of which accused no.2 was the Nominee, that had supplied the food article to accused no.1. Accused no.5 is stated to be the Manufacturing Firm, of which accused no.4 is the Nominee, that had supplied the food article to accused no.3. 2. As per the complaint, on 29.09.2008, the food officials consisting of Food Inspectors (FI) Chander Bhan Boora and Field Assistant (FA) J. S. Bisht under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Pradeep Baijal reached along with their staff at the premises of M/s. National General Store (Proprietorship concern of accused no.1), at 877, Multani Building, Qutub Road, Delhi-06, where the accused no.1 was found conducting the business of various food articles which were lying stored for sale for human consumption. The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of 'Culinary Sauce' from the vendor as lying in sealed plastic containers of 300 grams each bearing identical label declaration, to which he agreed. A sample of 3 such sealed containers of 300 grams each was then lifted and divided in three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules. Each sample was separately packed, fastened, marked and sealed and necessary documents were prepared at the spot, including the notice as per Form-VI, panchnama etc. The price of sample was paid to the vendor. Thereafter, one counterpart of the sample was sent to the Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA. Vide report dated 31.10.2008, the PA found the sample to be misbranded on the ground that it was giving misleading information regarding nature of article which was labelled as Mayonnaise (a proprietary item) as well as 'Culinary Sauce' (which was a standardized item and a fruit product). Upon receipt of report, the SDM/LHA ordered investigation which was carried out by FI. Various letters were issued by the FI to ascertain the details of the distributor and supplier. It was found that the accused no.1 had purchased the food article from accused no.3 Company that had in turn procured the same from accused no.5 partnership firm. Accused no.2 and accused no.4 were the Nominees of accused no.3 and accused no.5 respectively. After completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA. The complaint was then filed in the court on 25.02.2010 against all the accused persons alleging violation of section 2(ix)(g) and (k) of PFA Act, as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act. 3. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 25.02.2010. The accused persons appeared and filed an application under section 13(2) of PFA Act thereby exercising the right to get the second counterpart of the sample to be analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL). The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent for analysis to CFL. The CFL examined the sample and its Director gave Certificate dated 01.04.2010, opining the sample to be not conforming to the standards of 'Culinary Paste / Sauce' as per PFA Rules due to presence of acidity less than the prescribed minimum limit. 4. Based on the CFL report, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against all the accused persons on 09.06.2010 for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act, being violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/ 2 5. Subsequently, an application under section 19(2) of PFA Act was filed which was dispose of vide order dated 04.07.2014 and the benefit of warranty was granted to the accused no.1, 2 and 3 and they were acquitted of the charges. Subsequent trial was faced by accused no.4 and 5 and this judgement is with respect to these accused persons only. 6. At the trial, the prosecution examined two witnesses in support of its case. PW-1 FI C. B. Boora and PW-2 Sh. Pradeep Baijal were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings along with FI J. S. Bisht. Both these witnesses deposed about the proceedings conducted by them on 29.09.2008 and narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample of three sealed plastic containers of 300 gram each of 'Culinary Sauce', dividing it in three parts by treating one sealed container as one counterpart, fastening, sealing, marking the sample counterparts, and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses. They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A, notice Ex. PW-1/B, panchnama Ex. PW-1/C, notice under section 14A Ex. PW-1/D, raid report Ex. PW-1/E, PA Receipt Ex. PW-1/F and LHA receipt Ex. PW-1/G. PA report Ex. PW-1/H was received and investigation was conducted by PW-1. He sent various letters to various departments and the accused persons and sought their replies during the investigation. After completion of investigation, sanction Ex. PW-1/L was taken from the Director PFA and the complaint Ex. PW-1/M was filed in the court by PW-1. A copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-1/N was sent to the accused persons through post. These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel for accused no.4 and 5 wherein they denied that the accused persons had been falsely implicated or that a false complaint was filed. 7. Statement of the accused no.4 (also representing accused no.5) under section 313 CrPC was recorded on 17.10.2016 wherein he denied the allegations and pleaded innocence. He expressed ignorance about the sample proceedings as he was not present at the spot, though he denied the PA and CFL reports claiming that the product was as per standards. He did not lead any evidence in defence.
texts.arguments: 8. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused no.4 and 5 beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused persons have not been able to rebut the findings in the CFL report dated 01.04.2010 which as per section 13(3) of PFA Act is final and conclusive. It is submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony. It is a matter of record that vide statement dated 04.07.2014, accused no.4 and 5 admitted that the product in question as lifted from accused no.1 and as supplied to him by accused no .3, belonged to them. 9. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the sample proceedings were not conducted properly and that there are various contradictions and missing links in the testimony of witnesses. Ld. Counsel has strongly contended that there is variation in the reports as given by PA and CFL, which leads to conclusion that the two samples were not representative and therefore, conviction cannot be based solely on the basis of the CFL report. In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/ 3 10. 17. In Calcutta Municipal Corporation v. Pawan Kumar Saraf [AIR 1999 SC 738], it has been authoritatively laid down that the legal impact of a certificate of the Director of CFL is three fold: (a) it annuls or replaces the report of the PA, (b) it gains finality regarding the quality and standard of the food article involved in the case and (c) it becomes irrefutable so far as the facts stated therein are concerned. 18. In Subhash Chander v. State, Delhi Administration [1983(4) DRJ 100], it was observed by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi that "It has repeatedly been held by the supreme court that the certificate of the Director supersedes the report of the public analyst and is to be treated as conclusive evidence of its contents. For all purposes the report of the public analyst is replaced by the certificate of the Director.... It means obliterate, [LEAKAGE_MASK], annul, replace, make void, inefficacious or useless, repeal. It will be anomalous to hold that for some purpose it survives and for other purposes it is superseded." However, the defence strongly relies upon the judgement titled as Kanshi Nath v. State [2005(2) FAC 219], informing that the said ruling has been constantly followed by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in State v. Ramesh Chand [2010 (2) JCC 1250], Food Inspector v. Parvinder Malik [2014(2) FAC 306], State v. Vinod Kumar Gupta [2010(2) JCC 957], State v. Virender Kohli [2014(2) FAC 223], State v. Kamal Aggarwal [2014(2) FAC 183], State v. Vidya Gupta [2014(1) FAC 291], State v. Dinesh Goswami [2014(1) FAC 302], State v. Mahabir [2014(1) FAC 286], and State v. Santosh Sharma [2014(1) FAC 296]. It is submitted that comparison of the two reports would show that there are substantive variations which would show that the sample was not representative. 20. The Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Kashi Nath's case (supra), was dealing with a situation where there were certain variations in the reports of PA and CFL while analysing a sample of 'dhania powder'. Hon'ble Court considered the ratio in MCD v. Bishan Sarup [ILR 1970 (1) Delhi 518] and held that it would still be open for the accused to establish that the sample tested was not a representative one, and if the variation in the two reports is substantial enough, then the PA report can certainly be looked into to establish this variation. In Re vs A-1) Harish Kumar Ahuja on 19 October, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/164683348/ 5 21.
